Short version: the hour before bed matters more than total screen time. In a 2025 study of 1,200 kids aged 6 to 9, screens in the last 60 minutes meant falling asleep about 19 minutes later, worst with handheld devices and mildest with a shared TV, because of light, arousal from games and short videos, and lost wind-down time. What helped: a fixed screens-off time an hour before bed (weekends too), devices charged in the kitchen, TV in a shared room, and reading in the last half hour, with sleep back to normal in about two weeks; offer two books to pick from instead of a debate about minutes.
Action: Send you this summary as-is, and I can draft a one-line reply for Hannah's group chat if you want.

There's no single universal cutoff, but a common rule of thumb is that a retention curve has flattened when the period-over-period drop gets very small and stays small, for example under about 1 to 2 percentage points for three or more consecutive periods. Look at the slope rather than the level: a curve can flatten at 5% or at 40%. Also check it holds across several cohorts and that you're using a long enough window for your product's natural usage cycle.
Action: If you paste the cohort table, I'll check where it flattens using whichever threshold you pick.

In Canada an EFT is a batch electronic transfer (direct deposit or pre-authorized debit) through the clearing system, which is cheap, usually takes a day or more to settle and can be returned. A wire is a one-off, same-day or near-real-time transfer, costs more, and is generally final once sent. So sales shouldn't use them interchangeably: EFT is for routine merchant payouts, wire is for fast or large one-offs.
Action: I can draft a two-line definition for sales decks, and I'll confirm timing and fee specifics against what Lumen Pay actually offers before it goes in anything.

Generally no. In Ontario, landlords can't charge a damage deposit at all; the only deposit allowed is last month's rent (plus a refundable key deposit), and that rent deposit can't be used for scuffed walls. Ordinary wear and tear also isn't something a tenant pays for, and if the landlord claims real damage they have to go through the Landlord and Tenant Board. I'm fairly sure of this, but Diego should check the details of his lease and the LTB site.
Action: Draft a short message you can send Diego, with a pointer to the LTB and a line he can use with the landlord. I'll leave the LinkedIn job alerts as they are.

In short, an extended heat warning means the dangerous heat is lasting longer than a regular heat warning, so the risk of heat illness builds.
